body_markdown:
This story sounds more like a joke when you tell it. A car, some friends, and a piston-sized hole punched clean through their collective aspirations. The tale of woe is familiar to anyone who’s gone racing. But even if you know the feeling well, Lemons is far more cruel than most motorsport series: In Lemons racing, the competitors are the punchline.


I’ve been that punchline on many occasions. Hell, I’ve been racing the series (and a couple of its competitors) on and off since 2012. In that time, I’ve no doubt lit tens of thousands of dollars—and no fewer than two cars—on fire. It has brought me no appreciable spoils, let alone glory.


In case you’re not familiar, Lemons is a race series based on a simple premise: Take cars valued at $500 or less and pit them against a road course… for 24 hours. Hence the name, a play on the Le Mans 24-hour endurance classic. As with any racing series, regulations dictate what resources go into each build, and such restrictions breed ingenuity. With Lemons, however, the financial cap is so restrictive that—compared with other series—it’s insanity that often results.


Our BMW straight-six-powered C3 Corvette in its natural habitat: the paddock, with its hood up.


[Kyle Kinard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kkinard/)


The ruleset makes for the lowest graspable rung on the racing ladder, which means Lemons participation attracts misfits. The cars, people, and race officials—it’s an odd bunch all the way down.


I fit in perfectly, thank you.


Naturally, it’s the $500 “race cars”[that are particularly f***y](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/kinardi-line/kinardi-line-1-a-little-bit-fy/) , leading to a rate of attrition so high it’d make a WWI battlefield blush. Failure is expected, if not assured.


Why suffer? Why go Lemons racing in the first place? For me, the answer has always been simple: cost. It’s a doomed enterprise, but ultimately Lemons is the cheapest way on earth to take a legitimate crack at wheel-to-wheel endurance racing. The cost to step up to “proper” racing takes an order of magnitude more money. Given the choice between not racing and… whatever it is I do in a Lemons car, the choice is clear.


So, Lemons offers a relative bargain. Or at least it seems to. It’s still racing: at least $1000 per weekend, per head, to do it right. And that’s if you’ve already got the car and the infrastructure to tow and fuel the P.O.S.


Our team’s Mustang II has been shattering dreams for more than a decade, each iteration more ambitious and irredeemable than the last.


[Kyle Kinard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kkinard/)


I’ve found that even with all your ducks in a row, regardless of one’s preparation headed into race weekend, a Lemons car usually blows up or, if you’re lucky, runs like crap the whole time.


It means I’ve asked that ‘ *why’* question of myself many times in the roughly 15 years of racing Lemons. I’ve done so at least twice in The Year of Our Lord, 2026, when things were looking especially grim. Our race team’s first event of the year ended in predictable misery, just as it had during the final race *last* year. Two full race weekends that turned out to be merely race moments.


After an absolutely heroic late spring spent sourcing, sorting, and installing a new-to-us BMW S52 inline-six that “ran when parked,” I drove just three-quarters of a single lap of Pacific Raceways in late August before the valvetrain left the chat. Like the many stages of grief, Lemons triage follows a well-trodden path to despair.


On the weekend’s opening lap, I’d managed to limp our team’s[straight-six-powered C3 Corvette](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rhMSTPcSafI) near enough to the pits as the engine failed. From my first stab at the throttle as I merged onto the front straight, the BMW S52 seemed low on power. Like any good pilot, I flew the thing until it ran out of altitude.


“It’s probably a vacuum leak,” I shouted through my race helmet, after the car was towed back in the pits. “Did we get that line underneath the intake manifold plugged in?”


As always, the fix felt hurried and frenzied and vital at first, the sound of every other car but our own buzzing down the front straight. There was still the kernel of hope that *we* *might just get back out there.* So I groped underneath the manifold to check the fitting. The gloves and helmet came off. Then the suit. The tools came out.


In no time we ended up here:


If the tea leaves can’t tell you what’s wrong, consult the shop towels. They never lie.


Kyle Kinard


Yes, that’s Low Road Racing teammate and “[Camaro vs. World](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/camaro-vs-world/) ” superstar mechanic Levi performing a compression test with… some balled-up shop towels. Bent valves on three cylinders, it turns out. Day over. But the race weekend didn’t end in tears. Only a shrug and beers at the local Mexican joint. Laughter too. Life can only break your heart if you let it.


Of course, motor racing tends to break things. Endurance racing doubly so. While Lemons doesn’t (to my knowledge) run any 24-hour races anymore, the two-day sprint format, wherein your car runs on Saturday for eight(ish) hours and then again on Sunday for a bit less, tends to nuke hardware in short order.


For many years, the broken equipment broke me too. Oftentimes I flew back to my home state of Washington, from wherever I was living, to race with my buddies at The Ridge or Pacific Raceways. I funded the trips on airline points and a maxed-out credit card. More than once, my financial gamble was met with a car that either ran like crap or didn’t run at all. I’m not sure which is worse.


For years, I swore off Lemons because the financial juice, if you’ll pardon the awful pun, wasn’t worth the squeeze. I bought a budget race car with Levi to run in a BMW E30 spec series in the Pacific Northwest, hoping to “graduate” from Lemons for good. But Lemons’ gravity pulled me back in. The spec E30 has sat, and I’m back to spending my one or two precious race weekends per year chasing valvetrain gremlins with some of my best friends.


But now I do it with a smile on my face.


Alison Willmore, a critic for *Vulture,* once wrote a wonderfully perceptive[review of Jeff Nichols’s film The Bikeriders](https://www.vulture.com/article/review-the-bikeriders-shouldnt-be-this-uptight.html) . It’s a roughly two-hour film showcasing grown men who go off riding their beautiful motorcycles together, generally avoiding the outward expression of emotion as they grow closer together before falling apart. Think a *Boogie Nights* -style rise-and-fall kinda flick—with WAY more leather.


Zach, Felix, Levi, my co-owners in the Corvette. Do note the lack of leather biker jackets. We’re working on that.


[Kyle Kinard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kkinard/)


Willmore notes in her critique, “It’s \[…\] a movie that, more than anything else, is about men coming up with a hypermacho pretext to justify enjoying each other’s company.”


That line always stuck with me. At some point I realized the Lemons thing, for me, had become a lot less about seat time per dollar and a lot more about enjoying the company of my friends. I’ve got a family keeping me busy now and, frankly, I’ve lost more than a bit of my edge. My driving isn’t what it was, even if “what it was” wasn’t ever much at all.


A couple of weekends back, my band of Lemons teammates journeyed down to Laguna Seca to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the series. I couldn’t make it, but the race report came back in familiar tones.


Levi told me all about how my team’s race car lasted 70 laps before some unseen new ailment cropped up and shuttered the operation. The guys had hauled the car dozens of hours across two state lines to attend.


Another Lemons race down. Hundreds down the drain for a sticker on the helmet and a handful of memories worth remembering. Money well spent.


[Kyle Kinard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kkinard/)


Another failure, but the context between the lines—that was everything. I heard all about the team finally meeting Laguna’s historic curves, the odyssey to find an obscure engine part that led to an old barn full of 1950s Alfas, and that drive back up the coast on California’s good roads.


There was no frustration in Levi’s dispatch. Only the joy of a collective purpose shared among good friends, no matter how doomed the effort. Or maybe because the effort was doomed. I can’t tell the difference anymore.


I simply welcome the failure now. This misfit series for misfit cars, misfit racers, and misfit wrenchers is here to stay. Clearly. Finding my place among them—I call that a win.
